The Copper mahseer Neolissochilus hexagonolepis is a large cyprinid inhabiting fast-flowing hill streams of the eastern Himalayan region, where it supports important subsistence and recreational fisheries. Field surveys consistently indicate that females attain a total length at puberty of 23 centimeters [Lp = 23 centimeters], a size threshold that marks the onset of vitellogenesis in this species. In comparison, the maximum body size recorded for the species across its range reaches a remarkable 120 centimeters [Li = 120 centimeters] in total length, placing it among the largest members of the genus Neolissochilus. This ultimate length is achieved only after several years of sustained somatic growth in productive river reaches. The substantial size range between pubertal and ultimate length reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes extended growth after maturity, likely an adaptation to seasonal food pulses in montane torrents. Examination of ovarian biopsies from reproductively active females maintained under controlled conditions at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] revealed a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 10% [GSI = 10%].

The early life stages of the copper mahseer are characterized by a remarkably brief incubation period. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C] undergo hatching after just 19 days [ab = 19 days], a developmental rate that is notably rapid for a cyprinid of this ultimate size. The newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with a measured wet weight at birth of just 0.006 grams [Wwb = 0.006 grams], a mass derived from the modest egg diameter of approximately 2 to 2.5 millimeters. This minute birth weight represents less than one ten-thousandth of the mass the fish will eventually achieve as a fully grown adult. The rapid eclosion likely reduces the window of vulnerability for demersal eggs to predation and scouring during monsoon spates, while the tiny larval size obliges an immediate reliance on exogenous microzooplankton following yolk-sac resorption. Such a combination of rapid hatching and diminutive neonatal mass is consistent with a reproductive strategy that favors the production of numerous small offspring over fewer, more well-provisioned young. The time to sexual maturity is reached at approximately 1 year after hatching [tp = approximately 1 year after hatching].

As the young fish grow through the juvenile phase, their weight gain accelerates considerably, culminating in a maximum reported adult body mass of approximately 18,600 grams [Wwi = approximately 18,600 grams] for the largest individuals recorded. This ultimate wet weight was derived from length-weight regressions applied to the 120-centimeter (120 centimeters) [Li = 120 centimeters] specimens and underscores the species' capacity for substantial biomass accumulation in productive riverine habitats. The onset of female sexual maturation, however, occurs at a much smaller size. Females typically reach a wet weight at puberty of 126.5 grams [Wwp = 126.5 grams], a value that corresponds closely with the 23-centimeter length threshold and reflects the point at which females begin investing energy into egg production. The enormous disparity between pubertal weight and ultimate weight—a factor of nearly 150-fold—illustrates a life-history pattern in which reproductive activity commences early but somatic growth continues at a significant pace for many subsequent years. This strategy is common among large, long-lived freshwater fishes inhabiting unpredictable environments.

Longevity records for N. hexagonolepis indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 2,555 days [am = approximately 2,555 days] when reared under stable thermal conditions of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], equivalent to roughly seven years. This lifespan, while substantial for a tropical cyprinid, seems remarkably modest given the species' enormous ultimate body size and its slow approach to asymptotic mass. Such a compressed lifespan relative to other 120-centimeter (120 centimeters) [Li = 120 centimeters] fishes suggests that the copper mahseer follows a relatively fast-paced life history once the pubertal stage is passed, likely driven by high natural mortality associated with monsoonal flood events and fishing pressure. Captive fish have been documented to reach this age under standardized hatchery conditions at the same thermal regime, lending credence to the estimate. For comparative context, other cyprinids of similar adult size in Southeast Asian rivers, such as certain species of Catlocarpio, commonly live for two decades or longer. The much shorter lifespan observed in Neolissochilus hexagonolepis may reflect the higher metabolic costs of living in cool, fast-flowing montane streams.

The species' reproductive biology features a female total length at first spawning of 23 centimeters [Lp = 23 centimeters], a value that marks the transition to the adult spawning stock. Under hatchery conditions at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the gonadosomatic index of 10% [GSI = 10%] corresponds to a fecundity of likely several hundred eggs per spawning act, though precise clutch sizes have not been widely published. The small birth weight of 0.006 grams [Wwb = 0.006 grams] is consistent with a cyprinid that produces numerous batches of small eggs over a protracted breeding season coinciding with the post-monsoon period. This iteroparous strategy, wherein individuals can spawn multiple times across their roughly seven-year lifespan (2,555 days) [am = 2,555 days], buffers the population against recruitment failure in years of unfavorable flow conditions at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. Understanding these demographic parameters is critical for developing effective conservation and harvest management strategies, especially given the species' vulnerability to habitat fragmentation from hydroelectric projects across its Himalayan range.
